title: hello, internet.
text:
So… apparently I have a blog now and this is the official first post, the last one was just a small test.
I’m not entirely sure why.
Actually, that’s not completely true.
For a while I’ve wanted a place to write things down that doesn’t have to be a paper, a report, a presentation, or some other document that starts with a deadline attached to it.
I’m currently doing a PhD in complex systems, working mostly with higher-order networks, synchronization, and symmetry. This means I spend a considerable amount of time thinking about networks, staring at equations, writing code, and discovering that the thing I thought I understood yesterday is considerably more complicated today.
It has also somehow involved moving to Istanbul, spending time in Germany, traveling for conferences and workshops, meeting people from very different places, and dealing with all the slightly absurd situations that seem to come with academic life.
A lot happens during a PhD that never makes it into the final thesis.
And I think that’s the part I want to keep here.

title: hello, internet.
text:
so, what is this?
I’m not completely sure yet.
Part of this website will probably become a collection of research notes. I often realize that the best way to figure out whether I actually understand something is to try to explain it.
So there will probably be posts with titles like:
Okay, but what exactly is a hypergraph?
or
Wait, what’s a groupoid?
Mostly questions that at some point I had to Google myself, or asked to chatgpt haha.
But I also want to write about the rest of the experience: conferences, living abroad, academia, things that go wrong, things that unexpectedly work, and whatever else seems worth remembering.
Basically, somewhere between a research notebook and a PhD diary.

title: hello, internet.
text:
why now?
I’m writing this from Amsterdam.
I live in Istanbul.
I’m Brazilian.
And somehow this is a perfectly normal sentence in my life now.
That might be the best explanation for why I decided to start keeping a record of all this.
I don’t know how often I’ll write here, or what this website will eventually become.
But for now:

title: research
text:
My research is broadly about complex systems and nonlinear dynamics.
A question that keeps showing up in what I do is deceptively simple:
In networked systems, the way components interact can strongly constrain the collective behaviors that emerge. During my PhD, I’ve been exploring this question in the context of higher-order networks, with a particular interest in symmetry and synchronization.

title: research
text:
higher-order networks
Traditional networks represent interactions as links between pairs of nodes. This is an incredibly useful abstraction, but not every interaction is naturally pairwise.
In many systems, interactions can involve three or more components simultaneously. Higher-order networks provide a framework for representing these interactions explicitly, using structures such as hypergraphs and simplicial complexes.
A large part of my work involves understanding what changes — structurally and dynamically — when we move from ordinary graphs to these higher-order representations.

title: research
text:
symmetry
Symmetry provides a way of identifying parts of a network that are structurally equivalent.
For ordinary graphs, these symmetries can be described through graph automorphisms. In higher-order networks, things become more interesting: there are different ways of representing the same system, and the relationship between the symmetries of these representations is not always obvious.
I’m interested in understanding these symmetries, how they can be detected, and what they can tell us about the dynamics supported by the network.

title: research
text:
cluster synchronization
Synchronization doesn’t necessarily mean that every node in a system behaves identically.
Instead, subsets of nodes can synchronize with each other while remaining dynamically distinct from the rest of the network. This phenomenon is known as cluster synchronization.
One of the main questions I’m exploring is how these synchronized clusters relate to the structural symmetries of higher-order networks — including when symmetry predicts possible synchronization patterns and, perhaps more interestingly, when it doesn’t.

title: research
text:
beyond symmetry
Structure can tell us a lot about dynamics, but perhaps not everything.
Part of my current work is concerned with situations in which synchronized patterns cannot be explained by conventional automorphisms alone. This raises a broader question that I find particularly interesting:

How much can we actually infer about dynamics from structure alone?

Answering that requires looking beyond conventional symmetry descriptions and exploring more general ways of relating network structure to dynamically invariant patterns.

title: research
text:
research notes
I occasionally use the blog to write informal explanations of concepts, papers, or problems that I encounter while working on these questions.
These aren’t polished research results. They’re mostly notes from trying to understand things myself — which, I’ve learned, is usually when I understand them best.

title: about
text:
Hi! I’m Ricardo.
I’m a PhD researcher in complex systems, currently based in Istanbul and working on higher-order networks, synchronization, and symmetry.
I’m originally from Brazil, and my academic path has taken me through computational physics, applied mathematics, and now increasingly interesting questions about networks and collective dynamics.
I created this website mostly because I wanted a little corner of the internet to write things down: about research, academia, living abroad, and everything that happens during a PhD that never makes it into a paper.

title: about
text:
a little background
I studied Computational Physics at the University of São Paulo (USP) and later completed a master’s degree in Applied Mathematics, also at USP.
During my master’s, I spent six months in Germany working at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK). That period was also part of what eventually led me deeper into complex systems and nonlinear dynamics.
I’m now a doctoral researcher in the BeyondTheEdge project at Kadir Has University in Istanbul, where my research focuses on higher-order networks, synchronization, and symmetry.
Most of the time, this means trying to understand how the structure of interactions shapes collective dynamics — and occasionally wondering why a seemingly simple question has led me to another completely new branch of mathematics.
Outside research, I like bouldering — which apparently everyone does these days — and I’ve recently been spending way too much time playing Zelda.

title: about
text:
this website
This website is partly a research notebook, partly a PhD diary, and partly an excuse to keep a record of this slightly chaotic period of my life.
Some posts will be about things I’m learning. Others might be about conferences, living abroad, academia, or whatever strange situation the PhD has put me in that week.
No promises about a regular posting schedule.
